data.name: Erase_QuickDescription
data.value: Clears the partition tables and file system signatures, then creates a new file system. Takes seconds. The old data physically stays on the media and can be recovered with special software.

data.value: Overwrites every sector with a pattern and then reads the whole device back. Destroys the data and tests the media at the same time: finds bad sectors and counterfeit cards with fake capacity. The device is written and read in full, so this takes the longest.

data.name: Erase_PatternDescription
data.value: Random data differs in every sector, so the check proves that each sector really keeps its own data. Zeros cannot reveal a card that wraps addresses around.

data.name: Settings_ShowAllDescription

data.name: Settings_SkipFreeBlocksDescription
data.value: Free blocks of ext2/3/4 file systems are not read but stored as zeros: the image is created faster, and xz, gz and zst compress the zeros to almost nothing. The image is then not a byte-for-byte copy of the device: whatever lay in free space (deleted files, for example) is not kept, and comparing the image with the device shows differences there. Other file systems and everything outside partitions are copied in full, and so is an ext file system that was not cleanly unmounted.

data.name: Settings_UseBmapDescription
data.value: When an image has a .bmap next to it (Yocto's wic and bmaptool make one), only the blocks that hold data are written and compared, which is several times faster. The image is checked against the .bmap while it is written; if they do not match, writing stops before the partition table is written. Unlike bmaptool, everything outside partitions and the first and last mebibyte of each partition are always written, so an old boot loader environment or an old file system in an empty partition does not survive. The pages show which .bmap was found and let you turn it off for one image.

data.name: Settings_CreateBmapDescription
data.value: The .bmap (bmaptool format 2.0) holds the SHA-256 of the data, so the uncompressed image can be checked later. Together with skipping free ext2/3/4 space it also marks the free blocks as holes, and FlashTool or bmaptool then write the image many times faster.

data.name: Settings_DeviceTestDescription
data.value: Measures speed and finds unreadable areas and counterfeit capacity. Every test except reading destroys all data on the device, so the page is hidden unless turned on here.

data.name: Test_Warning

data.name: Test_Mode_ReadDescription
data.value: Reads the whole device, bypassing the Windows cache: speed along the device, the time of every request and the areas that cannot be read. Nothing is written.

data.name: Test_Mode_WriteVerifyDescription
data.value: Fills every sector with data unique to its position, then reads the whole device back. Finds counterfeit devices and their real capacity, bad areas and slow regions, and charts the speed of both directions. Takes as long as writing and reading the whole device.

data.name: Test_Mode_QuickProbeDescription
data.value: Writes small probes across the device and reads them back, then narrows down where data stops being kept. Takes minutes and catches the usual counterfeits; only the full test catches every kind.

data.name: Test_Mode_RandomAccessDescription
data.value: 10 seconds of random 4 KiB reads, then 10 seconds of random 4 KiB writes, one request at a time: what matters for a system running from the card (SD class A1/A2). The figures also depend on the card reader.

data.name: Settings_DifferentialWriteDescription
data.value: Before writing, each part of the device is read and compared with the image in 64 KiB blocks, and only the blocks that differ are written. The result is the same device as after a full write, with less wear, and faster when little has changed, for example when the same card is reflashed with a new build. Where hardly anything matches, comparing turns itself off for a while, because then it only adds time. The first part of the device is still cleared first and written last, and verification still reads everything back. Changing one file can shift the data of a whole file system, so the gain depends on how the image is built.
